The next morning the queue forms again, slower than usual. People step inside and stand a little closer than they need to, listening. Thomas knows what they are waiting for.

He lifts the first tray from the oven and lets his mind fill with the things it has always held. The smell of rye. The Hollis boy's birthday. How good it is to see them all. 'Lovely to see you, Mrs Pell.' 'Mind the step, it's icy.' Small, warm, perfect thoughts.

In Wickham's Rest they call it clean thinking. Children learn it before they can read: think gently, and you will never need to lie. There is no crime here. In twenty-six years of marriage, Thomas and Nell have never once argued.

By the third customer, shoulders loosen. By the tenth, someone laughs. The queue has forgiven him.

Only Thomas notices how tired he is by noon. Not from the baking. From the thinking.

find: Afternoon light weighs heavy against the stone walls of Wickham's Rest. Thomas stands by the lane, watching neighbors pass. A woman stops to greet a butcher, her lips curved into a warm smile. But beneath her words, her surface thought drifts out: "I cannot bear another hour on my feet." Then a micro-pause ripples through the air. The sentence catches, reverses, and re-forms into a bright broadcast: "The weather treats us kindly today." Now he can hear the effort. An editor in his head rewrites every thought before it forms, and he hears the same editor in everyone. At supper Nell thinks "what a lovely evening" while her face looks exhausted. He starts walking to the Line at night. Men and women walking by, husbands greeting wives, children running past—all of them running an internal censor, shearing away every jagged edge of fatigue and frustration before it reaches the air. Wickham's Rest is not peaceful because its people are gentle. It is peaceful because every mind in town works in a quiet panic.

In the afternoon he walks the bread round, as he has for thirty years. And now, because he is listening for it, he hears it everywhere.

Outside the butcher's, a woman greets a neighbour with a smile. Her thought drifts across the lane: 'I can't bear another hour on my feet.' Then a catch, the smallest pause, and the sentence turns over and comes back bright: 'The weather is being kind to us today.'

A man waiting by the post office: 'If he says that one more time, I'll...' A pause. 'Good of him to come.'

It is the same pause Thomas makes. A hand on the door before a thought is let out. An editor, working quietly behind every pair of eyes in town.

He stops in the middle of the lane, the basket heavy on his arm.

Nobody in Wickham's Rest has told a lie in forty years. But perhaps nobody here has been honest either. Perhaps they have only learned to edit.

For the first time in his life, Thomas wonders whether he would sound any different if no one could hear him.

The wind moves through the heather. Nell sits down beside him on the cold turf, close enough to touch, and for once he has no idea what she is thinking. It frightens him. It is also the first time in twenty-six years that she has felt like a stranger, and he finds that he wants to know her.

"Can I ask you something?" she says.

He nods.

"What do you actually think, Thomas?"

The question lands in the silence and stays there. Inside him the editor wakes at once and starts offering sentences. I think you're tired. I think we should go home. I think everything is fine. Gentle, true enough, and not one of them his.

He lets them pass.

He breathes in the cold air. He opens his mouth.

Behind them, the lights of Wickham's Rest go on burning, waiting for him to come back and be heard.
